title: Faricimab for Macular Edema secondary to Retinal Vein Occlusion: Real-world data from the University of Ulm
summary:
Information on Macular Edema (ME) in Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO)

Vision can be impaired by macular edema (ME) — an accumulation of fluid in the central part of the retina (the macula), which is often caused by a blockage in a retinal vein (RVO). After diabetic retinal disease, RVO is one of the most common causes of vision loss.
Treatment involves injecting medication directly into the eye (intravitreally). Until now, so-called VEGF inhibitors (Lucentis®, Eylea®, Avastin®) have been used. These agents block a protein that promotes the growth and leakage of blood vessels. Early treatment is recommended for the best possible outcomes.
Since June 2024, a new medication called Faricimab (Vabysmo®) has been available. It works via a dual mechanism by blocking both VEGF and another signaling molecule called Angiopoietin-2, which also contributes to vascular leakage and inflammation. Studies suggest that this combination may be more effective than standard therapy.
At the Department of Ophthalmology at Ulm University Hospital, Faricimab is used as part of a flexible treatment regimen known as "Treat-and-Extend".
This approach allows for personalized adjustment of injection intervals based on the individual course of the disease, aiming to make treatment more effective and less burdensome. The goal is to extend the time between injections and reduce the number of clinic visits. To further evaluate this new approach, clinical studies are planned at the Ulm University Hospital.

interventions.name: intravitreal injection of faricimab (Vabysmo ®) 120 mg/ml for refractory secondary macular edema in retinal vein occlusion, as “switch therapy” in pre-treated patients

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with macular edema (ME) secondary to retinal vein occlusion (either central retinal vein occlusion [CRVO] or branch retinal vein occlusion [BRVO]) who showed an insufficient response to prior anti-VEGF therapy with aflibercept (2 mg), bevacizumab, or ranibizumab were included. 

ME was considered refractory if intraretinal fluid persisted and central subfield thickness (CST) remained ≥ 270 µm despite receiving at least three anti-VEGF injections at intervals of no more than six weeks.
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria included any ocular disease other than RVO that could contribute to ME, ischemic maculopathy involving the fovea, disruption of the ellipsoid zone, iris or retinal neovascularization, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) worse than 1.3 logMAR, significant media opacities (e.g., cataract, vitreous hemorrhage), uncontrolled glaucoma, other vitreoretinal pathologies (e.g., vitreomacular traction, epiretinal membrane, or macular hole), previous vitreoretinal surgery, or any history of intravitreal steroid injection or implant.
